## Package Overview

`G2Gcov` implements maximum likelihood estimation, diagnostic plotting, and survival/retention trajectory forecasting of the Grassia(II)-Geometric (G2G) distribution for discrete-time duration data with both time-varying and time-invariant covariates and unobserved cross-sectional heterogeneity, following the methodology of Fader et al. (2019) and Fader and Hardie (2020). It also provides posterior updating given a customer's survival history, with posterior mean event probabilities and conditional survival forecasts.

| Function | Purpose |
|:---|:---|
| `G2G_varying_MLE()` | Maximum likelihood estimation with time-varying covariates |
| `G2G_static_MLE()` | Maximum likelihood estimation with time-invariant covariates |
| `print()` | S3 print method displaying estimates, SEs, Wald confidence intervals, and AIC |
| `plot_p0()` | Plot baseline per-period event probability density $p_0$ across the cohort |
| `G2G_varying_survival()` | Compute discrete-time survival function $S(t)$ along dynamic covariate paths |
| `G2G_varying_retention()` | Compute period-to-period retention function $r(t)$ along dynamic covariate paths |
| `G2G_static_survival()` | Compute discrete-time survival function $S(t)$ under static covariates |
| `G2G_static_retention()` | Compute period-to-period retention function $r(t)$ under static covariates |
| `G2G_varying_posterior_p0()` | Posterior mean of the baseline per-period event probability $p_0$ given a customer's survived covariate history |
| `G2G_varying_cond_survival()` | Conditional survival over planned future periods given a survived covariate history |
| `G2G_static_posterior_p()` | Posterior mean of a subject's per-period event probability given `hist` survived periods |
| `G2G_static_cond_survival()` | Conditional survival over `future` periods given `hist` survived periods |

---

## Time-Varying Covariates in the G2G Model

The G2G model is a discrete-time duration model in which the individual-level
per-period event probability is reparameterized as $p_0 = 1 - e^{-\lambda}$,
with $\lambda \sim \text{Gamma}(r, \alpha)$ across subjects to capture unobserved heterogeneity. Time-varying
covariates in period $j$, $z(j)$, enter via a complementary log-log link
with coefficients $\beta'$,

$$
p_j = 1 - \exp\left(-\lambda e^{z(j)\beta'}\right),
$$

which yields the closed-form survivor function

$$
S(t) = \left(\frac{\alpha}{\alpha + C(t)}\right)^r, \quad C(t) = \sum_{j=1}^{t} e^{z(j)\beta'}.
$$

The probability mass function (PMF) is:

$$
P(t) = \left(\frac{\alpha}{\alpha + C(t-1)}\right)^r - \left(\frac{\alpha}{\alpha + C(t)}\right)^r
$$

The likelihood function simply consists of the PMF and $S(t)$ for uncensored and censored subjects, respectively.

### Required Format for Time-Varying Covariates Data

Data must be in **person-period (long) format**:

* One row per subject per time period.
* A subject identifier column linking rows to the same individual.
* An event indicator equaling 1 in the period the event occurred, and 0 in all preceding periods. All 0s through the last observed period for censored subjects

| Column | Type | Description |
|:---|:---|:---|
| `id` | Identifier | Unique subject identifier (numeric, character, or factor) |
| `week` (or `time`) | Integer | Sequential discrete period index ($1, 2, 3, \dots$) |
| `status` | Binary (0/1) | 1 if the event occurred in that specific period; 0 in the preceding periods;  all 0s through the last observed period for censored subjects |
| `coupon, anyp, ...` | Numeric / Factor | Dynamic or static covariates (continuous, binary, or multi-level) |

Factor and character covariates are expanded into dummy variables through standard R formula mechanics (`model.matrix`, treatment contrasts).

---

## Example 1: Time-Varying Covariates (`kb_data`)

> **Note on Datasets:** To ensure this vignette builds rapidly within CRAN limits, we evaluate the models using `kb_data_sample`, a 20-subject subset of the package's full data intended for quick trials and interactive exploration. For full empirical analyses, simply use the entire cohort of 1,499 subjects via `kb_data<-G2Gcov::kb_data`. The syntax remains identical.

Each row in the data represents one customer-week. We print the first 50 rows to illustrate the person-period structure required for time-varying modeling.

```{r load-varying}
library(G2Gcov)
library(survival)

# Load the quick-start sample dataset
kb_data_sample<-G2Gcov::kb_data_sample

# Inspect the person-period data structure
round(head(kb_data_sample, 50), 2)
```

We estimate the model by directly supplying the formula and the subject identifier. Please note that both estimation functions require at least one covariate on the right-hand side of the formula.

```{r fit-varying}
# Estimate the discrete-time model with dynamic marketing covariates
fit_varying <- G2G_varying_MLE(
  Surv(week, status) ~ coupon + anyp,
  data    = kb_data_sample,
  subject = "id"
)

# View parameter estimates, standard errors, and Wald confidence intervals
print(fit_varying)
```

### Interpreting the Coefficients

Each coefficient $\beta_k$ acts on the complementary log-log scale, so $e^{\beta_k}$ is a hazard ratio: a one-unit increase in a numeric covariate, or a switch from the reference level to a given factor level, multiplies $\lambda$ by $e^{\beta_k}$. A positive $\beta_k$ raises the per-period event probability (shorter durations); a negative $\beta_k$ lowers it (longer durations).

The baseline per-period event probability, $p_0 = 1 - e^{-\lambda}$ with $\lambda \sim \text{Gamma}(r, \alpha)$, describes subjects at zero for numeric covariates and at the reference level of each factor. 

Hazard ratios are expressed per unit of each covariate, so raw coefficients are not comparable across covariates measured on different scales, such as `coupon` and `anyp`. To make an effect concrete, compute the hazard ratio for a meaningful change $\Delta$, $e^{\beta_k \Delta}$. An effect is distinguishable from zero when the confidence interval for $\beta_k$ excludes $0$ (equivalently, when the interval for the hazard ratio excludes $1$).

### Estimation Details

Internally, `G2G_varying_MLE()` applies several techniques to ensure robust numerical optimization:

* **Automatic Standardization:** To improve numerical stability and convergence of the BFGS algorithm, all continuous covariates are automatically standardized (centered and scaled) prior to maximizing the likelihood. Upon convergence, the resulting coefficient estimates are dynamically rescaled back to their original metric, ensuring the output is immediately interpretable on the scale of the original data.
* **Delta Method for Standard Errors:** The optimization routines estimate baseline parameters in an unconstrained space (e.g., using $\log(r)$ and $\log(\alpha)$ to enforce strict positivity constraints). The package computes the inverse Hessian matrix and applies the multivariate Delta method to derive standard errors on their original scale.
* **Wald Confidence Limits:** Using Delta method standard errors, the package automatically calculates and reports Wald confidence intervals: symmetric for the covariate coefficients, and computed on the log scale for $r$ and $\alpha$ so they remain strictly positive. By default, it reports 95% confidence limits, which can be modified via the `level` argument (e.g., `level = 0.99`).
* `G2G_static_MLE()` applies these same optimization and standardization techniques.

### Visualizations and Projections

We can visualize the implied distribution of the baseline weekly event probability across the population:

```{r plot-p0}
plot_p0(fit_varying)
```

> **A note on $r$ and $\alpha$:** The standard errors of $r$ and $\alpha$ can be as large as the estimates themselves, particularly in small samples. This is typical of a gamma mixing distribution and is not a sign of a problem: the two parameters are often highly correlated, because many $(r, \alpha)$ combinations imply very similar distributions of $p_0$. Interpret them jointly, for example through the implied distribution of $p_0$ shown by `plot_p0()`, rather than one at a time.

Next, we extract the survival curve explicitly using `G2G_varying_survival()` by passing a specific customer's covariate path, and plot the predicted step-function. The length of the generated survival curve aligns with the length of the covariate path provided: 

```{r plot-survival-varying}
# Predict individual survival curve S(t) along a specific customer trajectory
# (Subject 24 is included in our sample)
customer_path <- kb_data_sample[kb_data_sample$id == 24, c("coupon", "anyp")]

# Compute the survival curve predictions explicitly
surv_est <- G2G_varying_survival(solution = fit_varying, X_mat = customer_path)

# Plot the predicted survival curve using base R graphics
plot(
  seq_along(surv_est), 
  surv_est, 
  type = "s",  # Step function for discrete time
  col  = "blue", 
  lwd  = 2,
  xlab = "Week", 
  ylab = "Survival Probability",
  main = "G2G Predicted Survival Curve (Subject 24)",
  ylim = c(0, 1)
)
```

We can also project conditional period-to-period retention function, defined as $r(t) = S(t)/S(t-1)$,
along that same dynamic customer path using `G2G_varying_retention()`:

```{r retention-varying}
# Compute period-to-period retention r(t) = S(t)/S(t-1)
ret_est <- G2G_varying_retention(solution = fit_varying, X_mat = customer_path)

# Display 
head(data.frame(Week = seq_along(ret_est), Retention = round(ret_est, 4)))
```

---

## Example 2: Static Covariate Baseline (`survival::veteran`)

If covariates are fixed for each subject, the cumulative hazard simplifies. `G2G_static_MLE()` handles data in traditional cross-sectional format (one row per subject) and automatically manages factor variables like `celltype`. We demonstrate this using the `survival::veteran` dataset. 

```{r load-static}
vet <- survival::veteran
```

```{r fit-static}
# Using a 99% confidence limits in this example
fit_static <- G2G_static_MLE(
  Surv(time, status) ~ age + celltype,
  data  = vet,
  level = 0.99
)

# View parameter estimates and model convergence for the static baseline
print(fit_static)
```

We plot the baseline event probability distribution at reference covariate values (squamous cell type and age = 0). The first level of a factor is its reference category (here `squamous`). For `character` vectors, the first level is the alphabetically first value; use `relevel()` or `factor(x, levels = ...)` to choose a different reference:

```{r plot-p0-static}
plot_p0(fit_static)
```

Just like the time-varying model, we can project survival and period retention for a specific profile (passing original factor levels) using `G2G_static_survival()` and `G2G_static_retention()`. In this situation, we can also specify the length of these functions to be generated:

```{r plot-survival-static}
# Predict survival up to t = 150 days for a 49-year-old with squamous cell cancer
surv_static <- G2G_static_survival(
  fit_static, 
  data.frame(age = 49, celltype = "squamous"), 
  150
)

plot(
  seq_along(surv_static),
  surv_static,
  type = "s",
  col  = "red",
  lwd  = 2,
  xlab = "Days",
  ylab = "Survival Probability",
  main = "G2G Predicted Survival Curve (Static Profile)",
  ylim = c(0, 1)
)
```

```{r retention-static}
# Predict period-to-period retention across the first 10 days
ret_static <- G2G_static_retention(
  fit_static, 
  data.frame(age = 49, celltype = "squamous"), 
  10
)

data.frame(Day = seq_along(ret_static), Retention = round(ret_static, 4))
```

---

## Posterior Quantities Given Survival History

A customer who has gone several periods without the event has told us something about their own baseline rate $\lambda$: customers with a high $\lambda$ are less likely to still be around. `G2Gcov` turns this into two kinds of answers, for both the time-varying and the time-invariant model:

* the **posterior mean of the per-period event probability** after the observed survival history, and
* the **conditional survival probabilities** for the periods ahead, given survival through the history.

Throughout, the customer has survived (no event) through period $t$ with covariates $z(1), \dots, z(t)$, and $C(t) = \sum_{j=1}^{t} e^{z(j)\beta'}$ as before. The fitted $r$, $\alpha$ and $\beta$ are treated as known, and the covariates are assumed to be exogenous. The history supplied to the functions must therefore contain only event-free periods.

### Step 1: The posterior of $\lambda$

Given $\lambda$, the periods are independent, and the probability of surviving period $j$ is $\exp\{-\lambda e^{z(j)\beta'}\}$. Surviving the whole history therefore has probability

$$
P(T > t \mid \lambda, Z(t)) = \prod_{j=1}^{t} \exp\left\{-\lambda e^{z(j)\beta'}\right\} = e^{-\lambda C(t)}.
$$

Multiplying by the gamma prior density and dropping constants, the posterior of $\lambda$ satisfies

$$
\pi\big(\lambda \mid T > t, Z(t)\big) \;\propto\; \lambda^{r-1} e^{-\alpha\lambda} \cdot e^{-\lambda C(t)} \;=\; \lambda^{r-1} e^{-b\lambda}, \qquad b = \alpha + C(t),
$$

which is the kernel of a gamma density. Hence

$$
\lambda \mid T > t, Z(t) \;\sim\; \text{Gamma}\big(r,\; b\big), \qquad b = \alpha + C(t).
$$

The shape stays at $r$ and only the rate moves. The whole covariate history enters through the single number $C(t)$: a longer history, or a history under higher-hazard covariates, raises $b$ and shifts the posterior toward smaller values of $\lambda$.

### Step 2: A Laplace transform

For $\lambda \sim \text{Gamma}(r, b)$ and any $u > -b$,

$$
E\left[e^{-u\lambda}\right] = \int_0^\infty e^{-u\lambda}\,\frac{b^r}{\Gamma(r)}\,\lambda^{r-1} e^{-b\lambda}\, d\lambda = \frac{b^r}{\Gamma(r)} \int_0^\infty \lambda^{r-1} e^{-(b+u)\lambda}\, d\lambda = \left(\frac{b}{b+u}\right)^r .
$$

Both posterior quantities below are this expression evaluated at different values of $u$.

### Step 3: Posterior mean of the per-period event probability

If a covariate effect $m$ multiplies $\lambda$, the per-period event probability is $p = 1 - e^{-\lambda m}$. Its posterior mean is $1 - E[e^{-m\lambda}\mid \cdot\,]$, which is Step 2 with $u = m$:

$$
E\left[p \mid T > t, Z(t)\right] = 1 - \left(\frac{\alpha + C(t)}{\alpha + C(t) + m}\right)^r .
$$

For the **baseline** probability $p_0 = 1 - e^{-\lambda}$, the probability at covariate value zero, $m = 1$:

$$
E\left[p_0 \mid T > t, Z(t)\right] = 1 - \left(\frac{\alpha + C(t)}{\alpha + C(t) + 1}\right)^r .
$$

Two checks. With no history, $C(0) = 0$ and this reduces to the prior mean $1 - \left(\alpha/(1+\alpha)\right)^r$, the mean marked by `plot_p0()`. And the estimate falls as $C(t)$ grows, because surviving longer, or surviving under higher-hazard covariates, is evidence of a lower baseline rate.

### Step 4: Conditional survival over the periods ahead

Suppose the planned covariates for the next $s$ periods are $z(t+1), \dots, z(t+s)$, and let

$$
\Delta_k = C(t+k) - C(t) = \sum_{j=t+1}^{t+k} e^{z(j)\beta'}, \qquad k = 1, \dots, s.
$$

Given $\lambda$, surviving the next $k$ periods has probability $e^{-\lambda \Delta_k}$. Averaging over the posterior of Step 1 and using Step 2 with $u = \Delta_k$,

$$
P(T > t+k \mid T > t) = E\left[e^{-\Delta_k \lambda} \mid \cdot\,\right] = \left(\frac{\alpha + C(t)}{\alpha + C(t+k)}\right)^r, \qquad k = 1, \dots, s.
$$

This equals $S(t+k)/S(t)$ computed from the unconditional survival function, as it must. Taking $k = 1$ shows how the two quantities are related: one minus the first step is the posterior mean of the event probability in period $t+1$, namely Step 3 with $m = e^{z(t+1)\beta'}$.

### Why the Function Names Differ Between the Varying and Static Cases

The two cases ask the same question but not the same quantity, and the names reflect that.

| | Time-varying | Time-invariant |
|:---|:---|:---|
| Posterior mean function | `G2G_varying_posterior_p0()` | `G2G_static_posterior_p()` |
| Probability returned | Baseline $p_0$ (before applying covariates) | The subject's own $p$ |
| Value of $m$ in Step 3 | $1$ | $c = e^{x'\beta}$ |
| History input | Covariate path, one row per survived period | Number of survived periods, `hist` |
| Conditional survival function | `G2G_varying_cond_survival()` | `G2G_static_cond_survival()` |

**Time-varying case.** The covariates keep changing, and the covariates in force in the next period are a planning choice. The function therefore returns the baseline probability $p_0$, which is the same $p_0$ that `plot_p0()` draws and which does not depend on what happens next. It can be combined with any planned covariate path afterwards (this is what the conditional survival function does). The history still matters: it shapes the posterior of $\lambda$ through $C(t)$, but the probability returned carries no covariate effect for the periods ahead. The `0` in `p0` marks this.

**Time-invariant case.** The covariates are fixed, so there is no later choice of covariate values to leave open. A probability with the covariate effect stripped out would describe a subject who does not exist, and it could not be combined with anything else. The function therefore returns the subject's own per-period probability, $1 - e^{-\lambda c}$ with $c = e^{x'\beta}$. Because it is not a baseline quantity, the name drops the `0`. For a subject whose covariates are all zero ($c = 1$) the two coincide, and the static function returns the baseline probability. With a static history, $C(\texttt{hist}) = \texttt{hist}\cdot c$, so the posterior mean is

$$
E\left[p \mid T > h\right] = 1 - \left(\frac{\alpha + h c}{\alpha + (h+1) c}\right)^r, \qquad h = \texttt{hist}.
$$

This is also the probability that the subject has the event in the next period given survival through $h$ periods, which is one minus the first step of `G2G_static_cond_survival()`.

> **Note:** The functions condition on the fitted $r$, $\alpha$ and $\beta$ and ignore the uncertainty in those estimates. The values should be read as updates of the fitted model for one customer, not as intervals.

### Example: Time-Varying Covariates

We reuse `fit_varying` and `customer_path` from Example 1. Treating the first half of the customer's observed path as the survived history and the second half as the planned covariates for the periods ahead:

```{r posterior-varying}
# First half of the observed path = survived history; second half = planned path
n_hist      <- max(1L, floor(nrow(customer_path) / 2))
hist_path   <- customer_path[seq_len(n_hist), ]
future_path <- customer_path[-seq_len(n_hist), ]

# Posterior mean of the baseline p0 after the history, versus the prior mean
c(prior     = G2G_varying_posterior_p0(fit_varying),
  posterior = G2G_varying_posterior_p0(fit_varying, hist_path))
```

The posterior mean of $p_0$ is below the prior mean because the customer has survived. The conditional survival function then gives the probability of surviving each of the next periods under the planned covariates, given survival through the history:

```{r cond-survival-varying}
cond_surv <- G2G_varying_cond_survival(fit_varying, hist_path, future_path)

data.frame(AdditionalWeeks = seq_along(cond_surv) - 1,
           Probability     = round(cond_surv, 4))
```

### Example: Time-Invariant Covariates

We reuse `fit_static` from Example 2 for a 49-year-old patient with squamous cell cancer who has survived the first 30 days:

```{r posterior-static}
patient <- data.frame(age = 49, celltype = "squamous")

# Posterior mean of the patient's own per-period event probability
c(prior     = G2G_static_posterior_p(fit_static, patient, hist = 0),
  posterior = G2G_static_posterior_p(fit_static, patient, hist = 30))
```

Probability of surviving each of the next 10 days, given survival through day 30:

```{r cond-survival-static}
cond_static <- G2G_static_cond_survival(fit_static, patient, hist = 30, future = 10)

data.frame(AdditionalDays = seq_along(cond_static) - 1,
           Probability    = round(cond_static, 4))

# One minus the first step is the posterior mean event probability for day 31
all.equal(G2G_static_posterior_p(fit_static, patient, hist = 30),
          1 - cond_static[2])
```

* Fader, P. S., & Hardie, B. G. S. (2020). *Incorporating time-varying covariates in a simple mixture model for discrete-time duration data* (Research Note No. 037). https://brucehardie.com/notes/037/time-varying_covariates_in_BG.pdf
